articles.content: The co-director of An Eye for an Eye, Tanaz Eshaghian, reveals how she came to make a documentary about a woman facing the threat of execution from her husband’s family – as sanctioned by sharia law “Even though I was raised here,” says the Iranian-American film-maker Tanaz Eshaghian from her home in New York, “I was brought up with the understanding that there are things that you do and things that you don’t do.” Take her 2006 autobiographical feature, Love Iranian-American Style, about her experience of dating in her 20s, which was, she says, “about how I was supposed to marry a nice Iranian man and stay a virgin”. But by the time she’d graduated from Brown University in Rhode Island “that ship had sailed”, she laughs. Since Love Iranian-American Style, she has made equally taboo-breaking documentaries about a women’s prison in Afghanistan (Love Crimes of Kabul, 2011), trans people in Iran (Be Like Others, 2008) and disabled teenagers in Pakistan (As Far As They Can Run, 2022). And with each new project, the duality of her heritage (Eshaghian emigrated to the US not long after the Iranian revolution when she was six) has spurred her to focus eastwards, closer to where she was born. “When you’ve been raised in the west you can see how similar the thinking is,” Eshaghian says of the similarities she’s found there: “the conservative thinking, the place of women, what’s allowed, what’s important”. Continue reading...

articles.author: Eloise Cooke
articles.content: A new exhibition celebrates landmark artists who sliced up existing works to make striking new pieces. The show’s curators discuss how, in order to create, sometimes you first need to destroy When Valerie Solanas sold her SCUM Manifesto in 1967 it was priced at 10 cents for women and $1 for men. Artist Justine Kurland considered doing something similar with her “man books”: sell them off cheap to undermine their cultural weight. But knowing that people would just flip the books for a profit, instead she took a knife to what she calls the “problem of language and history and inheritance” in photography. She went through her own library of canonical male photographers, cut up the books and made collages from the spoils. Kurland called the project SCUMB (Society for Cutting Up Men’s Books), after Solanas’s manifesto. The same idea underpins What Rose from the Cut, a group show at Graces Mews Gallery in south London. Co-curated by Kurland, the V&A Parasol Foundation curator of women in photography Fiona Rogers, and collector Sarah Miller Meigs, the show brings together more than 40 artists working in collage, photomontage and assemblage, across three generations. All the artists share a simple aim: to make something new out of something already there. The result is no one thing: the show is erotic, sentimental, irreverent and sobering, often all at once. “There is something very specific to the idea of what it is to tear something apart,” Kurland says. “There are so many things that collage immediately does right out the door.” Continue reading...

articles.author: Devi Sridhar
articles.content: Protein is the food industry’s current nutritional good guy. The fact that it’s often added to ultra-processed food makes it anything but When I was growing up in the US in the 1980s and 90s, fat in foods was demonised . Low-fat yoghurt, low-fat desserts and low-fat margarine were all the rage, with the message that fat was bad for our hearts and arteries . By the early 2000s, concern had moved to added sugar and its apparent links to obesity and type 2 diabetes , driving food reformulations. Sugar was replaced with artificial sweeteners such as aspartame and acesulfame K, which have their own health impacts. Aspartame is classified by the World Health Organization as possibly carcinogenic in humans, while observational research such as a 2022 study of about 102,000 adults has linked acesulfame K with increased cancer risk. Then carbohydrates came into the spotlight, with pasta, rice and bread becoming the bad guys for our diet and blamed for weight gain. There is a fashion cycle in nutrition, where each food group or ingredient takes its turn being blamed for our poor health. Prof Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of Edinburgh Continue reading...

articles.author: Ed Aarons
articles.content: Crystal Palace’s influential supporters’ group disbanded 24 hours before their first home game this season – and Selhurst Park has not been the same since Simon Teesdale could not help feeling mixed emotions when his beloved Crystal Palace won the Conference League in Leipzig in May. He started going to Selhurst Park with his father in the 1980s, became a season-ticket holder in the 1990s and has watched with pride as the club established itself as a permanent fixture in the Premier League over the past 14 years. Palace finally secured a major trophy in the 2025 FA Cup final – an experience Teesdale remembers as “one of the best days of my life” – and followed that up by winning the Conference League but he decided in August not to renew his season ticket. “Something happened between the FA Cup win and today that changed me,” he wrote in an emotional article published last month on his website. “Tipped me over the edge. Actually, it’s fairer to say that something accelerated in that period of time. The seeds were sown years ago.” Continue reading...

articles.author: Daniel Dylan Wray
articles.content: Backed by the KLF, a monument is being built using 34,592 bricks, each containing a deceased person’s glazed ashes. Is this the future of funerals? We join emotional marchers on Birkenhead’s smoky, noisy Day of the Dead Hundreds of people wearing hi-vis clothing are on a death march through Birkenhead Park. A burning shopping trolley leads the way, smoke grenades clog the air, and people holding traffic signs chant: “The dead don’t stop – till they reach the top.” There’s a wave of curtain-twitching from residents who look on with fear and bemusement as what looks like a psychedelic building site gone rogue marches through their beautiful recreation space. Where could they be going? The answer might shock some of them. For this crowd are on their way to build a pyramid … made of dead people. “My brother calls it my ‘anarchist death cult,’” laughs Steve Lowe, chief engineer of L-13 Light Industrial Workshop, who is involved in running Birkenhead Day of the Dead and the People’s Pyramid. It’s an event that has taken place every year (except 2020) since 2018 in a variety of locations and was announced by Jimmy Cauty and Bill Drummond of the KLF (AKA the Justified Ancients of Mu Mu AKA K2 Plant Hire Ltd), the seminal electronic duo and experimental art provocateurs, when they returned after 23 years in 2017. Continue reading...

articles.author: Chris Wiegand
articles.content: A wave of shows, including High School Musical and Rent, are upping the drama by placing viewers alongside actors at the heart of the action. What are the risks and rewards? In the socially distanced summer of 2020, Jesus Christ Superstar was staged at Regent’s Park in London for a hugely pruned audience. Like the actors, we were kept two metres apart. It was a triumphant but extremely strange experience – not least from my current perspective. I’m standing on stage at Theatre Royal Drury Lane, jostling alongside other theatregoers, watching a miraculous revival of the same production. But this time, 75 audience members have been given a spot within the scaffold-style set for the show, beneath the musicians and almost side by side with the cast. We feel the energy of the ensemble’s dance moves, seem to join the crowd of Jesus’s followers – and those who conspire against him – and come extraordinarily close to the musical’s star, Sam Ryder, who rests right by my feet after his solo Gethsemane. It’s as close as I’ve been to the beating heart of a big West End production. Until, that is, the following week when I watch the captivating revival of Rent at the Tom Stoppard theatre from one of 82 audience seats arranged in a semicircle on stage. (Mine is just beneath a shelf bearing candle-filled wine bottles – a marker of La Vie Bohème.) Stranger Things’ Gaten Matarazzo bounds past on to the stage, the actors mingle with us and the band are only just out of reach. Continue reading...

articles.content: The beautiful and mercenary Honey is a monstrously compelling character, in a novel with the ruthlessness of Richard Yates but more wit ‘A sweet white grape of a book” is how Virginia Woolf described Elizabeth Jenkins’s first novel, Virginia Water, published in 1929 when Jenkins was 24. Jenkins may have detected a condescending note. She was wary of Woolf, having been invited into the Bloomsbury inner circle and then (in her own view, at least) just as quickly dropped again. Jenkins soon regretted the novel’s publication, apparently afraid acquaintances might recognise themselves, and tried to get rid of as many copies as she could. Fortunately she wasn’t long deterred, either by her uneasy dealings with Woolf or her anxiety about Virginia Water; her subsequent literary career spanned 70 years, though most of her books had fallen out of print by the time she died in 2010. Perhaps this reissue of her 1968 novel, Honey, will bring Jenkins back into fashion. It ought to. Continue reading...

Fortunately she wasn’t long deterred, either by her uneasy dealings with Woolf or her anxiety about Virginia Water; her subsequent literary career spanned 70 years, though most of her books had fallen out of print by the time she died in 2010. Perhaps this reissue of her 1968 novel, Honey, will bring Jenkins back into fashion. It ought to. Continue reading...
articles.title: Honey by Elizabeth Jenkins review – a rediscovered 60s classic of sex, money and power

articles.author: Jon Bryant
articles.content: Market stalls are laden with local delicacies in the run-up to Christmas, while the city’s elegant cafes make the perfect spot to sit and watch the world go by Famous for its fabulous fruit and vegetable markets, Aix-en-Provence extends its stalls in winter to include les treize desserts de Noël , the 13 desserts of a traditional Provençal Christmas. I buy almonds (which represent the Carmelites), dried figs (Franciscans), walnuts (Augustinians) and raisins (Dominicans) from the Place Richelme market. Then I queue up in the Place des Prêcheurs for oreillettes (sweet, ear-shaped wafers), gingerbread, and white and black nougat (representing good and evil). Calissons d’Aix, the city’s celebrated, lozenge-shaped sweets, come from the smart Brémond or Le Roy René confiseries nearby. These desserts are laid out on tables in Provençal homes for the Christmas period interspersed with santons (tiny clay figurines), which are sold at Aix’s Foire aux Santons from mid-November. Also displayed alongside the usual Nativity figures in the churches and tourist office, these feature hundreds of Provençal characters including bakers, wet nurses, beekeepers, a pétanque player and the artist Paul Cézanne, who was born in the city, all grimacing to reflect the drudgery of daily life. In January there is even a nativity play, La Pastorale Maurel , at Aix’s Théâtre du Jeu de Paume, with humans playing the still-grimacing santons. Continue reading...

articles.author: Zoe Williams
articles.content: Deprivation is behind the sharp rise highlighted in the Natsal study, and that’s an outrage. High energy bills should never be a factor in reproductive choice The National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal) is the crowdpleaser of the data world. Nerds love it because of its extraordinary thoroughness. It’s one of the largest studies of sexual behaviour in the world, surveying nearly 7,000 people in the UK between the ages of 16 and 59, once a decade. Everyone else loves it because they get to talk about sex. Some of the statistics speak for themselves – among 25- to 34-year-old women, the number who say they never want children has gone up fourfold, a sad, completely understandable reflection of the outside world. Other figures, though, are mysterious: the number of women aged 16 to 24 who are on the pill has dropped precipitously , from nearly half to less than a third. Over the same period, the online space has been flooded with information about hormonal contraception, some of it better than it has ever been – more accessible, more accurate – and some of it plain wrong. Is there strategic, funded disinformation coming from Christian fundamentalists, such as we have already seen in the abortion space, where anti-abortion activists hose money at putatively “grassroots” online influencers ? Or is it a quirk of the algorithms that once you go down the rabbit hole of “has the pill made me depressed?”, you will be shown endless influencers who have experienced that very (improbable) thing? It’s hard for a young person to navigate what’s real, and it’s hard to distinguish superstition from preference. articles.author: Rachel Roddy
articles.content: Soft, plump, sweet-savoury rolls marry historical English breakfast baps with a culinary tradition from Italy’s mountainous Trentino-Südtirol In Elizabeth David’s English Bread and Yeast Cookery , there’s a chapter called “Manchets, Mayn and Payndemayn”, all of which were 15th-century names for rarefied soft white bread made from the finest wheat flour. As well as pages of historical context that only she could make so lively, David includes a 1615 recipe for manchet from a book called The English Huswife that calls for meal to be ground into the whitest flower, mixed with ale yeast, salt and liquor (a mixture of water and milk), before being wrapped in a cloth, kneaded with feet, left to swell, shaped, then baked in a gentle heat. It is this form of manchet that David sees as being the common ancestor of all English breakfast breads: baps, soft rolls and dough cakes, with the presence of milk (and, therefore, fat) ensuring both crumb and crust are soft. In fact, her recipe for breakfast baps (or, rather, a recipe from Mr CG Lockyer from Crewkerne) is almost identical to manchet, although without the millstones, dough tub and feet. Continue reading...

articles.author: Mona Chalabi
articles.content: I thought making a will would be easy. Somehow, I ended up grilling my friends about their finances I’ve spent a lot of my life thinking about death. When I was six, my dad had a heart attack. He had been our primary caregiver – the person who took us to school, took us to play in the park and bought us takeaways (the sweet man’s skills didn’t extend to the kitchen). The day it happened, my sister and I were rushed to A&E so we could see him lying wordless in a bay in case he didn’t live. Though he did survive, he never recovered and the threat of death hung over the household. It delivered on its promise when I was 18. Rather than feeling relief that his suffering was over and the purgatory of sickness was done, I turned to worrying incessantly about the health of my mother. Because my parents were immigrants, they had no family in Britain – no one they could ask to watch us for a couple of hours without payment, let alone look out for us after they were gone. So, just before I started secondary school, my mum asked one of my friends’ parents if she could name them as our next of kin. They said yes, but not wanting to rely on others, she continued to work hard to ensure we, as well as her family in Iraq, would have as much financial security as possible. Continue reading...

articles.content: Photographer David Levene meets service personnel and veterans at selection trials in Lviv for next year’s Invictus Games in Birmingham It took a little longer than expected for the 100 or so archers to begin competing inside the large Soviet-era velodrome arena at MoD SKA in Lviv (built for the 1980 Moscow Olympics, it is Ukraine’s only indoor cycling track) on the first day of trials for the team that Ukraine will send to next year’s Invictus Games in Birmingham . The delay gave competitors a little extra time to stretch and practise. Coaches paraded up and down the line, giving some last-minute advice on strategy and technique to the waiting men and women facing down their targets. Pavlo and Vadym share a laugh during the laser tag trials. Pavlo lost his left leg from a landmine in 2023 and swimming became his path to physical and mental recovery. Vadym suffered a frontline injury in 2022. He set a Ukrainian record for runners with below-knee amputations, completing the 42km Marine Corps Marathon in 3hrs 30m in October 2026. Continue reading...

articles.author: Kirsty Major
articles.content: Luyen Vu’s discount eye surgeries represent the dangers of an unregulated beauty industry. But for her fans, she is a folk hero Robert Laycock, a facial plastic surgeon at Aintree University Hospital in Liverpool, first knew that something was up when a patient came to him in early 2024. She was a woman in her 40s who had undergone a blepharoplasty, a procedure that involves making an incision just below or above the eyelids and removing small amounts of skin and sometimes fat and muscle. The point of the surgery is to make the patient’s face look more youthful. This woman’s stitches, however, had started coming apart, leaving an open wound right above her eyes. It is not unusual for botched private cosmetic surgeries to be fixed on the NHS. Laycock estimates that he sees three or four patients a year who need surgical intervention after too much tissue has been removed in a blepharoplasty. But something was different about this woman. “The surgery was done in a very odd way,” Laycock told me. The incision, he explained, had been made just beneath the eyebrow rather than on the crease of the eyelid. “[It’s] not the way that we would generally do a blepharoplasty in the UK.” He asked the woman where she’d had the work done but she was evasive and he dropped the subject. Continue reading...

articles.author: Alex Needham
articles.content: He’s been pierced, chained, inflated, stretched, suctioned and denounced in the Senate. As Ron Athey hits the UK, he talks about his upbringing in ‘a cult’ – and why being naked just isn’t enough ‘The nicest way to say what I do is that I want to create a miracle,” says Ron Athey. “The gnarly way is that I know what the edges are when it comes to the mortification of the flesh.” The softly spoken performance art legend has come to the Guardian’s offices in a flat cap and navy blue Fred Perry hoodie. Only his facial tattoos and platform boots hint at the fact that he has been responsible for some of the most extreme works of live art of all time. Take Self-Obliteration, which begins with a naked Athey violently brushing a long blond wig pinned to his head with blunt needles, before tearing it off, upon which blood pours down his face and on to his body. (Blunt needles, you see, make bigger holes.) Or Solar Anus, in which he puts hooks in his face that stretch the skin of his cheeks and eyes, turning his face into a kind of ancient Egyptian death mask. In St Sebastian, Athey is suspended by chains while assistants pierce his flesh with arrows and needles. Continue reading...

articles.author: Hannah J Davies
articles.content: The star was chewed up and spewed out by the tabloids after the Sun on Sunday sting in 2013. But she is disarming in this fight for change – and ready to ‘raise a bit of hell’ In 2011, Tulisa Contostavlos was at the peak of her powers. At 22, the N-Dubz singer turned solo artist had landed a coveted position as a judge on The X Factor, stepping into Cheryl Cole’s towering stilettos. As she puts it here, her pitch to X Factor supremo Simon Cowell was simple: “You’re gonna need someone to sit there and look pretty and cry when [there are] emotional moments, and you’re gonna need someone to tell people they’re rubbish when they’re rubbish – and I’m gonna do both.” Cowell hired her on the spot, she says. Tulisa was a household name, but sections of the British media treated her with contempt, with headlines that played up her working-class background and labelled her a chav. Much of this three-part series is concentrated, however, on the most egregious example of the press turning on her: a sting by the Sun on Sunday in 2013, which saw Tulisa groomed into believing she was auditioning for a Hollywood film over the course of several months. Eventually, she was asked to supply drugs to a producer, and – under pressure to please her new bosses – passed a phone number to the infamous Sun journalist Mazher Mahmood, AKA The Fake Sheikh. Continue reading...

articles.content: Federal judge Loren L AliKhan grants preliminary injunction in ABC’s favor after network sued FCC in August The federal judge Loren L AliKhan on Wednesday granted a preliminary injunction blocking the Brendan Carr-led Federal Communications Commission (FCC) from taking any action curbing ABC’s ability to renew its broadcast licenses, after the network sued the agency in August over an unusual demand to apply early to renew the eight local licenses for stations it owns. The FCC claimed that the early renewal process was necessary to procure documents related to an ongoing Diversity, Equity and Inclusion (DEI) investigation, but the network countered that it was being punished for editorial coverage that was deemed critical of the Trump administration. The FCC’s order came after Donald Trump and the first lady, Melania Trump, criticized ABC for a comment made by the late night host Jimmy Kimmel. Continue reading...

articles.content: The guitarist was absolutely integral to Duran Duran’s success, and not merely because he was by far the band’s most straightforwardly talented musician Andy Taylor, guitarist in Duran Duran, dies aged 65 Andy Taylor – a life in pictures It’s very easy indeed to paint Andy Taylor as the misfit within the world-beating five-man line-up of Duran Duran. The others were fans of glam and Chic: their avowed intention was to form a band that melded the sophisticated disco of the latter with the extravagant style and experimental art-pop of Roxy Music. Taylor – who had made what he later called “that fateful journey down to Birmingham” from his home on Tyneside after spotting an ad in the Melody Maker – had tastes that tended towards rock music of a more traditional stripe, as evidenced by the artists he covered on his second solo album, 1990’s Dangerous: Thin Lizzy, Bad Company, AC/DC, Montrose. Continue reading...

articles.content: From a half-time huddle gone wrong to an ultimatum over play-calling, here’s what the quarterback said Wednesday in a scorched-earth appearance on Pat McAfee’s show Barely 12 hours after the Pittsburgh Steelers announced that Aaron Rodgers would be deactivated and Mason Rudolph would start Friday’s game against the Denver Broncos, the four-time NFL Most Valuable Player left no bridge unburned in a surprise call-in to ESPN’s The Pat McAfee Show. In a 34-minute appearance on Wednesday afternoon where he spoke uninterrupted for long stretches, Rodgers accused Steelers head coach Mike McCarthy of falling asleep in a quarterback meeting, skipping walkthroughs and falling behind on film study. He also said the 63-year-old McCarthy broke a half-time huddle against Philadelphia with the words “One, two, three, Packers”. According to Rodgers, McCarthy denied falling asleep at the team facility. Continue reading...

articles.content: Wired, wireless, noise cancelling and budget … here are the headphones to level up your PC and console gaming • The best gaming chairs We talk a lot about graphics in video games; we know how important it is to play on a decent screen so we can see what we’re shooting at … or running away from. But what about sound? Explosions, dialogue, the wheezy breathing of a nearby monster – arguably, audio quality is just as important. Many modern games now support 3D or spatial audio, which lets you detect exactly where a sound is coming from in the game world. In survival horror adventures, you can hear the zombie lurking in the next room, and in popular shooters such as Fortnite and Apex Legends, you can pinpoint the footsteps of approaching enemies. Continue reading...

articles.content: Andy Burnham needs a radical vision of economic change to move on from policies aimed at giving voters ‘breathing space’ Ask Andy Burnham a question and it won’t be long before he mentions the cost of living. Responding to the results of midterm elections in the US earlier this month, he said that the Democratic party’s triumph meant that there was “an opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all, and that’s the cost of living”. This wasn’t a non sequitur. The Republicans lost control of Congress in large part because Donald Trump failed to address concerns about the cost of basic goods – a failing aggravated by the US president’s disastrous war against Iran, which caused a spike in commodity prices, exacerbating the affordability problem. articles.author: Editorial
articles.content: The UK must continue to oppose the UAE’s tainted nominee, Lana Nusseibeh. The ethical course is also the pragmatic one The future of the United Nations has rarely looked more perilous in an age of impunity for atrocities, raging wars, open US hostility, a funding crisis and security council deadlock. It is widely agreed that the choice of its next secretary general is critical – perhaps even existential. Unfortunately, that’s where agreement ends. Under the opaque selection system, security council members are privately polled on their views of each candidate. A “discourage” vote from one of the five permanent members is diplomacy-speak for a veto. Only when a consensus emerges does the general assembly get a say on the candidate. The next straw poll is due on Monday, with no deal yet in sight . With António Guterres completing his term on 31 December, the seat could fall empty for the first time. articles.content: It feels as if we’re destined to hold the same referendum every decade. Nige, Arron and co are up for the fight Roll back the years. The Bad Boys of Brexit have reformed and are back in town. Andy Wigmore on comms. Arron Banks on lead vocals and money. Nigel Farage on doing whatever the hell he likes. Apart from spending his own cash on security. This time round, though, a woman has joined the band. Step forward, Catherine McBride. Probably the only woman alive who Nige thinks he can trust not to be totally pissed by 3pm. Even so, you can sense that this is a relationship destined to end in tears. Give it a couple of months and Catherine will be wishing she had never met Nige and Arron. Continue reading...

articles.content: Readers on the failure of the climate talks in Turkey and the lessons we can learn The failure of Cop31, as commented on by Bill McGuire ( A year of deadly floods and fires – and yet Cop31 still collapsed. When will our leaders grasp the scale of this crisis?, 24 November ), is the expression of the overwhelming momentum of the value system of a global culture that is wedded to the seemingly unstoppable expansion of our material production and consumption. The disjunction between peril and necessary action is explained by the impossibility of taming appetites that are insatiable. It is convenient to blame fossil fuel producers, and while they are obviously guilty parties, the ultimate problem is the continuing demand for their products. Continue reading...

articles.content: Raymond T Pierrehumbert and Dr Lynne Jones respond to an article by the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh Watching Miatta Fahnbulleh, the secretary of state for energy security and net zero, forced to defend the government’s retreat from net zero ( Where do people want to see Britain’s climate action plan working? On their own doorstep, 17 November ) was painfully reminiscent of the way in which Colin Powell, a former US secretary of state and an honourable man, was forced to defend George W Bush’s claims justifying the disastrous Iraq war. Fahnbulleh states that people need to see the benefits of net zero on their doorstep – meaning jobs, cost of living and warm homes. But in fact the policies of this government mark a retreat of all of these “doorstep” benefits. Andy Burnham has slashed heat pump subsidies , which means more vulnerability of homes to heating price shocks from international affairs spiking fossil gas prices; it also means fewer warm homes and jobs in the heat pump manufacturing and installation industry. Continue reading...

articles.content: To distort what was actually a reduction in supply into a reduction in demand and then use it as ‘evidence’ is unworthy of our world-class research institution, says Marcia Saunders After a cyber-attack in 2023 , which Ciaran Martin, a former CEO of the National Cyber Security Centre, described as “ one of the worst cyber incidents in British history ”, use of the British Library’s reading rooms fell dramatically ( British Library to outsource security and ‘repurpose’ reading rooms as business spaces, 20 November ). Throughout 2024-25, services were heavily affected, including archives, manuscripts, books and online journal articles. All readers’ tickets were suspended and initially were reissued for limited periods of time. It should surprise no one that use of the reading rooms fell off. Only last month was access to the UK web archive (partially) restored. Continue reading...

But amid the praise for the architects who masterminded this transformation, and the well‑aimed barbs at the City of London Corporation, which tried to prevent it, there is no mention of those who provided the all-important funding. articles.content: Measles is spreading across the world and could give rise to another pandemic, writes Colette McIvor After reading your report ( ‘They’re struggling for oxygen’: children pay the price as countries allow measles to surge again, 20 November ), I was struck by the statement that proposed cuts to foreign aid from wealthy countries are likely to exacerbate the problem, particularly for those within developing countries. The UK intends to cut foreign aid spending from 0.5% to 0.3% of national income by the end of 2027. Worryingly, in its 2025-26 report, the Foreign Commonwealth and Development Office proposed a cut of 35% on funding provided to the Democratic Republic of Congo . As your article pointed out, the DRC is already experiencing a deadly Ebola outbreak; with the spread of measles, thousands more will be lost to a different, and largely preventable disease. Continue reading...

articles.content: (Atlantic) Justice bring some 80s nostalgia but this compilation of new material from music’s A-list – from Dua Lipa to Travis Scott and a host of Latin talent – stays at the cutting edge It can be hard to ascertain why Grand Theft Auto VI is such a phenomenon from merely watching along with it. Equally devoted to the thrill of a violent crime story and a more mundane lifestyle fantasy, the appeal does not always translate to bystanders. Its soundtrack, however, is another story: a compilation of brand new material from some of the biggest pop, rap, rock and country artists on the planet – some of them combined in imaginative pileups of guest features – that can be enjoyed totally separately from the gameplay, if you so wish. Starting from Zero, the opener by Justice – also composers of the game’s original score, released on 11 December – features the unmistakable voice of the Doobie Brothers’ Michael McDonald belting out an 80s-style pop ballad complete with a saxophone outro. This style is synonymous with Grand Theft Auto VI’s setting, a fictionalised version of Florida last seen in 2002’s Grand Theft Auto: Vice City, which was beloved for its inclusion of 80s hits. Continue reading...

articles.author: Ben Eastham
articles.content: White Cube Bermondsey, London Kiefer asks what art means after the Holocaust – but even the vast scale of his powerfully seductive paintings can’t do justice to the gravity of his themes When the world is falling apart, the artist retreats to the studio. It’s an old story, and Anselm Kiefer has always loved the old stories, drawing for his monumental and reliably blockbuster paintings on narrative traditions ranging from Norse mythology to German Romantic poetry. So it makes sense that an artist who has dedicated his life to the question of what art means after the end of European civilisation – which is to say, after the Holocaust – should now seek out the solitude of the studio to make sense of what’s coming. Kiefer’s exhibition at the same gallery a decade ago had the title Walhalla , after the beer hall in the sky in which dead Vikings drink away the afterlife. Now comes the more modest (you would think) subject of the artist’s studio, depicted here in a suite of lustrous landscapes and a simple wooden cabin in the forest. Rendered in flat gold leaf, the sky in these paintings gleams like a tarnished halo in an old altarpiece, while the verdigris grass pushes roughly off the canvas. Here is the place where heaven meets the earth and is transmuted – by the alchemy of this painter’s touch – into quietly numinous paintings containing elements of both. If you can put aside the fact that Kiefer’s own studio is a vast warehouse complex on the outskirts of Paris, these paintings present a very German vision of communion with nature. They also evoke the most famous hut in modern philosophy: the Black Forest hideaway where Martin Heidegger formulated his argument that “authentic” culture must be rooted in the native landscape. The flipside of this idea, that nature is not just a scenic backdrop to human history but a living participant in it, would have, let’s just say, consequences for German painting after 1945. Here is the challenge that Kiefer has spent his career meeting: how to paint the landscape as an unspoilt refuge from society when it is littered with mass graves? Continue reading...

articles.author: Arwa Mahdawi
articles.content: A war correspondent interviewed 100 sources about the pop star, but what does the 4,500-word story reveal? If you are extremely online you will have known for a while that a big takedown was coming. An exposé of a well-known blond billionaire, a powerful figure that people are terrified to criticise, was in the works at a large publication. A former war correspondent had been assigned the story! A hundred sources had been interviewed! The reporting had taken a year! The truth would finally out! For everyone else, let me explain in plain English. On Monday Vanity Fair published an eagerly anticipated, 4,500-word piece, about Taylor Swift called The Mastermind. While it was labelled as “commentary”, it was framed as a deeply sourced piece written by May Jeong, a journalism professor at Princeton who has won awards for her reporting from Afghanistan. Continue reading...

articles.author: Ben Fisher in Istanbul
articles.content: Unai Emery wanted the winger but, like Harvey Elliott last season, he has been left out in the cold despite Villa’s attacking struggles It is three years this week since Alejandro Garnacho opened the scoring for Manchester United in a 3-3 draw at Galatasaray in the Champions League, on a typically boisterous night in Istanbul when Victor Lindelöf and Aaron Wan-Bissaka, now his teammates at Aston Villa, were also among the starters. At the time, Garnacho was a teenage star flourishing on the grandest of stages, a fixture in the United team and fresh from scoring an outrageous overhead kick at Goodison Park a few days earlier that would later clinch the Premier League’s goal-of-the-season award. He went on to score twice at Old Trafford on Boxing Day, in a 3-2 victory against Villa, and a couple of months later his double at home to West Ham was the catalyst for that iconic celebration photo of Garnacho, Kobbie Mainoo and Rasmus Højlund sitting on the advertising hoardings at the Stretford End, beaming smiles all round. All three were at the heart of United’s plans for a bright future, beacons of hope. At the end of that season, Garnacho signed off in style, he and Mainoo scoring against Manchester City at Wembley to win the FA Cup . Continue reading...

articles.author: Andrew Sparrow
articles.content: Pair clashed at PMQs over a video shot outside No 10 by TikToker Max Balegde Diane Taylor is a Guardian reporter who covers migration. Britons get many of the facts about migration wrong and Reform UK voters are the group who get these facts most wrong, according to new research published today by King’s College University and YouGov. Among Reform UK supporters, 57% think net migration rose significantly in the year to June 2025, compared with 11% of Labour supporters and 8% of Greens. Eight in 10 Reform supporters think that asylum seekers are prioritised for social housing, compared with 21% of Green supporters. It is wrong to believe that if we could only correct misperceptions, we would automatically reduce concerns about immigration or policy preferences – because that misdiagnoses a large part of the cause, that these divides are partly driven by deep differences in values and identity. Continue reading...

articles.author: Emma Brockes
articles.content: For all the fuss, it makes perfect sense for the PM to engage young people through TikTokers. He’ll have the last laugh on this one These are dangerous times to be a prime minister. So it is perhaps reassuring that the trouble into which Andy Burnham barrelled this week is so old school as to be almost soothing. Four months into his premiership, Burnham has arrived early at that rite of passage: the catastrophic attempt to engage with popular culture and subsequent category-5 storm in a teacup. After footage emerged of Influencers Behaving Badly at Downing Street, Burnham, in my view, has come out of the whole thing in surprisingly good shape. To recap: earlier this month, Burnham held a reception for social media influencers, one of whom, Luke Hamnett , was permitted to film himself doing the Hugh Grant dance from Love Actually before sitting down to interview the prime minister. Meanwhile, self-described “presenter, podcaster, idiot” Max Balegde filmed himself outside the door of No 10 miming what, in the words of the Daily Mail as it geared up to go the full Judge Pickles, “appeared to be a viral meme song”. These words were “bomboclaat pussywagon chicken nuggets”, which, as the Telegraph took a breath from its own meltdown to explain, turns on “a Jamaican profanity popularised online”. Emma Brockes is a Guardian columnist Continue reading...

articles.author: Nesrine Malik, in East Jerusalem
articles.content: Despite militarisation, occupation and marginalisation, African culture prevails in the Old City, something I discovered first-hand when I visited Don’t get The Long Wave delivered to your inbox? Sign up here In occupied East Jerusalem, I met an often overlooked community: African Palestinians. This week, I explore their unique history, and how they are, in a classic diaspora fashion, integrated and marginalised in equal measure. There are about 450 African Palestinian people in occupied East Jerusalem, mostly living in the historical buildings of the Old City, near al-Aqsa mosque. That mosque, the third holiest site in Islam after those in Mecca and Medina, is the reason they are there. While Christians make up a small part of the African Palestinian population, most African Palestinians descended from Muslim pilgrims who came to East Jerusalem in the early 20th century (before Israeli occupation), and stayed either to tend to the mosque, or to continue Islamic practice and devotion within the city’s religious ecosystem. Continue reading...

articles.content: From a choreographed summit that dominated Westminster but barely registered in Brussels to a climate showdown in Turkey, last week revealed the EU’s priorities – and the limits of its collective power • Don’t get This Is Europe delivered to your inbox? articles.content: Life100 features the wisdom of two women in their 80s and has gone viral by exploring important life lessons It is, unfortunately, a familiar scene. At the dinner table, a woman berates her granddaughter with invasive, personal questions – why are you still single? Anyone who has been in this situation likely knows what comes next. The granddaughter may try to deflect, only to invite further questioning, or call out her grandmother’s rudeness, which risks escalation. Continue reading...

Early in the second half of Tuesday night’s National League South match between Torquay United and Chesham, play was briefly suspended due to an ear-splitting din emitted over the Plainmoor public address system. “The game has stopped because the Torquay Tannoy system is making a loud noise that won’t stop,” posted Chesham on their Social Media Disgrace account. “I’m not kidding.” A sort of aural cross between an ocean liner’s foghorn and a party conference speech delivered by a senior member of the Reform party, it eventually stopped and play resumed with Torquay running out 2-1 winners. Given the precedent of awarding/revoking/re-awarding of the Afcon 2025 edition this would be entirely justified” – Peter Martin. This is an extract from our daily football email … Football Daily. articles.author: Brian Logan
articles.content: SEC Armadillo, Glasgow The comedian’s new concoction, Vaudevillean, mixes offbeat historical diversions, topical gags and virtuoso musical flights with warmth and absurdity Is any act ever really too niche for stardom? What could be more leftfield, after all, than Bill Bailey’s animated pop-musicology, with demonstrations on the Swedish nyckelharpa and the one-stringed Indian lute? But tonight he has yet another arena crowd hanging on his every strum, drumbeat and twang. Nothing need be niche, perhaps, if communicated with the open-hearted curiosity and passion Bailey brings to his esoteric interests. Add a flair for improbable juxtaposition, and a sense of humour that dusts curmudgeonliness with surrealism, and you’ve got a concoction that thousands-strong audiences find difficult to resist. The 61-year-old’s current show is called Vaudevillean, and gestures are made towards justifying that title, with reference to the French poet Olivier Basselin and the 1453 battle of Castillon. (You don’t get this with Michael McIntyre.) Like vaudeville, the show certainly has variety to recommend it. But really, this offering differs little from many a previous Bailey outing , and finds our host again following his nose from one unlikely musical experiment to another, via nuggets of topical standup and anecdotes from his storied life. Touring Europe until 2 May Continue reading...

articles.author: Keith Stuart
articles.content: Rockstar’s latest blockbuster makes the everyday business of shopping, working out and taking care of a pet snake as compelling as its shootouts and car chases I knew I’d need many skills during the opening hours of Grand Theft Auto VI, but effective time management was not one of them. From playing the previous five titles in the series (and their many spin-offs), I understood I’d have to master Rockstar’s idiosyncratic approach to car handling. True enough, the vehicles do drive like airbeds tied on top of supermarket trolleys. I also knew I’d need to get to grips with the somewhat tricky aiming and shooting if I was to commit any sort of respectable crime spree. But for the first few hours of playing this staggeringly large and bewildering game, what concerned me most was lead character Jason’s personal routine. Each day, he needs to get up, choose an outfit, complete a workout, feed his pet snake Dolores, and perhaps do some DIY, so that when his girlfriend Lucia gets out of jail she’ll fall for him again – rather than fall through his apartment’s rotten staircase. Meanwhile, his drug-smuggling boss phones every five minutes with new parcels for Jason to pick up or drop off, and his pals Cal and Donnie get into all sorts of cocaine-related hijinks they expect Jason to extricate them from. There are also predatory neighbours to do favours for, and groceries to buy. I’ve seen so many people on social media posting about how they took several days off work to play this game, only to find themselves busier and more productive than ever. On his radio show last week, James O’Brien derided himself for completing, in Jason’s apartment, a simple DIY task that he’s put off for months in his own home. I know where he’s coming from. Continue reading...

articles.content: Daily global surface temperature hit record 2.24C above baseline levels on Monday and streak is forecast to continue For the first time, the world has experienced six consecutive days of temperatures 2C warmer than preindustrial levels, the Guardian has learned. This record hot streak , which is continuing, is too brief to signify that the upper range of the Paris climate agreement target has been breached, but scientists said it was an early indication of what is to come unless fossil fuel emissions are rapidly eliminated. It is also likely to feed into growing scientific concerns that global heating may be accelerating . Continue reading...

articles.content: While referees tend to reach for red early in the season before easing off, players are under increasing pressure to keep pace in a frenetic environment Off! Off! Off! The past three Premier League games have featured a red card, each for a different reason. Brighton’s Costinha was sent off for two bookings at Hull , Leny Yoro collected a red card against Liverpool for denying a goalscoring opportunity ( though his suspension was overturned on appeal ) and James Tarkowski saw red for serious foul play at Brentford . This season is shaping up to be an outlier in the VAR era of officiating in English football. The latest red cards took the Premier League total to 22 in 2026-27. The rate of 0.2 per game equates to 76 across the whole season, which would equal the Premier League record set in 2005-06. Refereeing has evolved in the past decade, though. The average across the seven completed campaigns since VAR was introduced is 0.12 per game, with a high of 0.15 in 2023-24. Continue reading...

articles.content: A generation known for loneliness is putting their own spin on a millennial-made tradition that requires socializing It’s a TikTok scene straight out of a stress dream: two men stand in their freshly cleaned apartment, explaining how all but one of the people they invited to Friendsgiving flaked out at the last minute. There is a can of whipped cream on the table and a 6lb ham in the oven. According to the video, posted by pop-culture podcaster Jackson Strike, those who ditched were either tired, or sick, or had a difficult day at work. More than 1.5 million people liked the video and many flooded to the comments section to express their disappointment at what they saw as an epidemic of antisocial behavior. “Everyone wants a village until they have to be a villager,” one user wrote. “Time to get new friends,” quipped another. Continue reading...

articles.author: Jess Cartner-Morley
articles.content: From a V-neck sweater worn back-to-front to a perfectly framed collarbone – here’s the secret to low-stakes sex appeal I’m not sure when it started being not chic to want to look sexy, but it’s definitely a thing and it bothers me as it doesn’t feel truthful to the human experience, if that’s not a lot for the first sentence of a fashion column. Our wardrobes have become shrines to good taste. Well-cut coats and quality knitwear, elegant flat shoes and crisp white shirts. These clothes are excellent at communicating that you have read the briefing notes for the meeting and have some Booker prize chat. They are less good at suggesting you might be up for dancing on a table later. Why do we have to choose? Clothes have always been partly about how they make us feel physically. We accept that an outfit can make you feel powerful, cool, smart. Why shouldn’t it also make you feel hot and fun? Continue reading...

articles.content: Read Darkroom by Meher Iqbal – this year’s winner of the Guardian and publisher 4th Estate’s award for unpublished writers of colour Meher Iqbal wins 2026 4thWrite prize with ‘evocative’ coming-of-age story • Content warning: This story includes a description of a sexual assault Nadia and I lay on the asphalt road, playing our favourite game for the last time. My older brother Abdullah had taught it to me when I was nine: lie down on a speed bump, legs long and both arms outstretched by your ears, making your body a long pencil. I was in the wrong position that day – it was so hot that the backs of my shins seared when they touched the road, so I had to bend my knees. Nadia wasn’t allowed to have her legs exposed anymore, so her linen trousers protected her. The game was intuitive – when you hear a car coming, roll down the slope and run away as fast you can. If you turned around only to find that the car was a decent way away, you were a baby. Abdullah never explained the underlying objective to me, but I think he enjoyed how much it agitated and scared adults at the same time. Simple and stupid, like most things he taught me at that age, but I liked that it gave me an opportunity to see just how fast I could run; the 100-metre track at school never drew out of me what running for my life did. Nadia didn’t care about any of that, but she humoured me anyway. Continue reading...

articles.content: Wildfires and floods can do little to move climate change up voters’ list of priorities, experts say Beneath the blackened branches of a pine tree that rises high above a landscape of scorched hillsides and the odd charred and ruined house, two older men address the obvious. Four months after one of the summer’s many wildfires threatened to devour the hamlet of El Morro , an hour west of Madrid, local people are still counting the cost and awaiting compensation. “Look at that house,” said Esteban Pérez, pointing to one of the properties that did not make it through July’s flames. “Everything inside is scorched, completely destroyed. You can still see the windows, but they’re gutted. The entire structure of the house next to mine had to be torn down, too. And they’ve given the owner nothing so far.” Continue reading...

articles.author: Peter Bradshaw
articles.content: DuVernay’s follow-up to her dissection of the 13th Amendment to the US constitution is a vehement and exhilarating defence of democracy Ava DuVernay’s previous documentary 13th , energised by the Black Lives Matter movement, was a brilliant polemic about the 13th Amendment to the US constitution , which she argued perpetuated a link between slavery and prison for African American men. Ten years later, and after an almost continuous decade of Trumpism, DuVernay has made a follow-up film about the 14th Amendment , and she has evidently arrived at a rather different attitude to the constitution and its authors’ intentions and good faith. Now she sees the enemy as Maga and the constitution as something that must be defended against a tinpot bully president and his viper’s-nest court of sycophants. The shift in view is not acknowledged, but the overall effect is similar. Utilising a gallery of very smart talking-head interviewees, including conservative Republicans, DuVernay has mounted a vehement and exhilarating defence of what might be called the second American Enlightenment, created by the 13th, 14th and 15th “reconstruction” amendments, drawn up between 1865 and 1870 after the American civil war. The 14th specifically established birthright citizenship, due process and equal rights for all races under the law, and furthermore barred insurrectionists from holding public office, all of which Trump appears casually intent on vandalising, airily amnesiac about his oath to uphold the constitution. Continue reading...

articles.author: Sid Lowe in Madrid
articles.content: Englishman hailed by teammates and manager Mourinho after coming on to completely change Champions League game against PSV Eindhoven “It was one of those moments when you’re just: ‘Wow.’” Bernardo Silva had a good view of Jude Bellingham scoring the goal, the golazo , that put Real Madrid into the lead and the Bernabéu on its feet, shock giving way to song, naa, naa, naa, na-na-na-naa, na-na-na-naa ringing round again. “I have no idea what I did,” the Englishman said afterwards. What he did was turn all Le Tissier. Lifting the ball with his left, raising it with his right, twisting and not letting it drop, he sent it arching from the outside of his boot into the far corner, something straight out of the 90s. “I just kind of hit it,” Bellingham reckoned; not wanting to hit it too hard, it had gone “looping”, “stabbing”, he said. “Normally [my goals are] a lot closer, aren’t they? I was a bit surprised, honestly. Normally from there I’m looking to see who is an option to play it through to, but it popped up nicely. It was nice.” Nice? It was, Silva said, “special”. A “work of art” Marca called it. The presenter on one radio station claimed it was the best goal he had ever seen, and it wasn’t just him; wasn’t just the goal, either. Continue reading...

articles.author: Osasu Obayiuwana in Lagos
articles.content: After African football was dragged into needless disrepute the next step is to tackle two key areas of governance A journey of 310 days and three legal proceedings to confirm two things we know – that Senegal beat Morocco 1-0 to win the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations and, most importantly, that the decision of a referee remains final and sacrosanct – has produced the longest, most comical and embarrassing Afcon final in the tournament’s 69-year history. As the Confederation of African Football (Caf) executive committee member Samir Sobha told the Guardian, the decision of the organisation’s appeals board in March to overturn Senegal’s victory and award the title to Morocco, prompting a legal charade ended by the court of arbitration for sport’s verdict on Tuesday , was a “big joke” that brought Caf and the Afcon into needless disrepute. Continue reading...

articles.author: Tom Service
articles.content: Rob a bank to the sound of Sibelius, mow down an alligator to the music of Mahler … piano sensation Yuja Wang is one of the surprises of GTA VI – and her thrilling musical choices made me crash into a G-Wagen I blame Yuja Wang for crashing my car. You know how it is, you’re cruising as fast you can on the freeway, listening to Symphony FM. And then DJ Yuja says: “It’s afternoon here in Vice City: for the worst of you, the day is just starting. Maybe the next piece will inspire you to turn your life around.” And then she played Tchaikovsky – the finale of the Fifth Symphony – and I just lost it to the music. The energy and tempest of the finale turned me into a driving maniac, and I ended up crashing into a G-Wagen down a one-way street as the minor-key maelstrom took over. Thanks Yuja. I’ll send you the repair bill. Such are the hazards of discovering that among the 24 stations you can listen to in Grand Theft Auto VI – and not only in your car – is Symphony FM, hosted by the in-game Yuja, who really is the real-life piano superstar Yuja Wang . And in choosing her “favourite pieces and curating a playlist for players to discover”, she’s put together a set of 16 pieces that only she could have come up with. Continue reading...

articles.content: Caitlin brings her ultimate comfort food to the table: a celebration of carbs and dairy. From teenage music journalist to bestselling feminist author, Caitlin Moran has spent her life asking questions, challenging convention and making us laugh along the way. She's interviewed rock stars, changed the conversation around feminism and written some of the funniest observations about modern life. She reveals what it was like growing up as the eldest of eight children in a home-schooled, unconventional family, learning to cook from library books. She also looks back on her teenage years as a music journalist, touring with the likes of Radiohead and the Beastie Boys, her early experiences of fame and the making of How to Be a Woman. Plus, she opens up about her relationship with food and body image, and how she came to recognise and eventually let go of the anxiety she once thought was essential to her creativity. New episodes of Comfort Eating with Siobhán are out every Wednesday. Continue reading...

articles.author: Emine Saner
articles.content: The Great White Hope, All the President’s Men, Kramer vs Kramer … Alexander has a CV most actors can only dream of. She talks us through the highs and lows – including a ‘beautiful’ encounter with Muhammad Ali Jane Alexander will never forget the play that won her a Tony award, a husband and her first film role. The Great White Hope, which ran on Broadway from 1968 to 1970, was based on the life of Black boxer Jack Johnson, who in 1908 became world heavyweight champion in segregated America. Alexander played Eleanor, a white woman married to an African American boxer also called Jack, at a time when interracial marriages were still illegal in many states. Decades later, when the play opened, the US supreme court had only recently struck down all remaining bans – and Alexander received hate mail and death threats for the role. Continue reading...

articles.author: John Duerden
articles.content: The coach will leave early after the postponement of the Asian Cup and, while there has been clear progress, some had hoped for better results at World Cups A popular Christmas tradition in Japan is to head to KFC but there is an unexpected item on the menu to chew over this year for the millions who do so – a meaty debate over Hajime Moriyasu’s eight years as national-team head coach. Among the many consequences of the Asian Cup’s postponement from January 2027 to December is the fact his tenure has ended early. The 58-year-old was supposed to stay on until February to cap that lengthy spell with (hopefully) a deserved trophy, hand over to Go Oiwa and then, perhaps, blaze a trail to Europe. Instead he left this month, after 113 games in charge during which Japan became a global force to be reckoned with, even if there are those who think he underdelivered. Continue reading...

articles.content: Groundsman on 15-hour days across finals weekend England in home dressing room against All Blacks The Rugby Football Union’s head groundsman is confident Twickenham’s pitch will hold up to staging six matches across three days for the Nations Championship finals, detailing the lengths to which he and his support staff will go. In preparation for the showpiece weekend, the turf – which had been in place since 2012 – was ripped up over the summer with a new state-of-the-art hybrid surface laid. It comes complete with a reservoir that can hold 1.4m litres of water below it – which can be reused using nanobubble technology – and was grown in Scunthorpe before being transported to south-west London. articles.author: Sadiq Khan
articles.content: Another day and, despite all the promises, another damning report on the Met. There will be a reset: the public won’t be brushed off any more and neither will I In March 2023, Baroness Louise Casey published her damning review into the Metropolitan police. The review – which I commissioned after a series of appalling scandals – called for systemic reform to a failing organisation unable to tackle the profound problems it faced. But yesterday’s independent follow-up report by Dr Gillian Fairfield shows that, while the Met has made some important improvements, nowhere near enough has been done. I agree. Fairfield’s report concludes that the Met remains institutionally racist, sexist and homophobic. This will be acutely concerning for communities across the capital. So, too, will evidence of the Met’s failure to treat many victims of crime with care and compassion at the very moments they need it most. Sadiq Khan is the mayor of London Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in our letters section, please click here . Continue reading...

articles.author: Phil Hoad
articles.content: The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth is the latest in a growing wave of movies steeped in nostalgia for a heyday in stark contrast to its current ruination If Los Angeles was a person, it might just be a laid-back fiftysomething trouper with cool sunglasses and an even better haircut. Some dodgy episodes in his past, but still handles himself with style. In other words, Los Angeles personified is Cliff Booth – the over-the-hill stuntman played by Brad Pitt in Once Upon a Time … in Hollywood , now turned studio fixer in the sequel, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth. Set eight years later in 1977, Further Mis-Adventures is more plot-driven, more Elmore Leonard-esque than the pure expansive “memory piece” of Once Upon a Time. But both films are steeped in the ambience and lore of old LA, drawn in part from Quentin Tarantino’s memories of cruising around the streets aged six in his stepdad’s Karmann Ghia (the car Booth also drives). They’re part of the recent intensely nostalgic LA revivalist mini-boom of work that also includes Paul Thomas Anderson’s Licorice Pizza (2021), Damien Chazelle’s Babylon (2022) and Ti West’s MaXXXine (2024). Continue reading...

articles.author: Florence Hallett
articles.content: The artist adorns her luscious paintings with diaristic notes and confessions. Ahead of an exuberant new show she discusses their unique creation method – and the hunt for her missing cat The artist Michaela Yearwood-Dan is on the hunt for her missing cat. Pinto disappeared from her home in east London a couple of weeks ago and has so far defied the forecasts of tarot readings and the “witchy ladies” predicting his return. A lost pet is not the only thing she’s searching for. “I’m at a stage of life where I’m looking for answers” she says on the eve of her exhibition The Practice of Liberation, at Towner Eastbourne. Her other, more existential questions are those of many women in their early 30s: “Do I want to have children? How do I want to have children? What does my future look like?” She is “big into astrology”, but recently her thoughts have turned to her Catholic upbringing in south London, which serves as a large theme of her exhibition, which debuted at the Whitworth Gallery in Manchester earlier this year. Religious ritual has always appealed to her, and her show uses paintings, ceramics and a musical composition by her friend and longstanding collaborator Alex Gruz to evoke the ritual space of a church. Continue reading...

articles.content: We point to self-care as we skip out on activities – but routinely staying home poses its own risk to our mental health You might have heard by now, but Americans are quite lonely , especially if they’re young. The kind of low-effort, high-frequency hanging out we used to rely on – dropping by for dinner, meeting up at the park, watching each other’s kids – has all but evaporated from our lives, leaving us unmoored from the social fabric that underpins our most basic wellbeing. (For reference, chronic loneliness has a comparable impact on long-term health to smoking .) Continue reading...

articles.content: Small children do not appreciate it when you join in with their singing or throw away their pee-covered leaves. And only a brute would suggest one of them might be tired Nobody can be good at everything, can they? Take me, for example. While I excel at remembering useless facts, going down online rabbit holes and getting toothpaste on my shirt, my singing is so bad it makes small children cry. This is not hyperbole: my five-year-old has wailed on many occasions throughout her short life because I’ve had the temerity to sing along to various TV show jingles or songs. As it turns out, however, it may not just be the fact that I can’t hold a tune that’s upsetting her. I’m not saying that everything I know about parenting I learned from viral posts on the internet, but there was an illuminating tweet doing the rounds last week that said: “Today I learned if you try to sing along with a toddler when you have not been invited to do so, it is a sign of great disrespect in their culture.” I immediately went down an online rabbit hole and discovered various other people have made similar jokes . It’s a common issue. Continue reading...

articles.content: Ahead of him rounding out the year at a huge London show, the DJ legend will join us to answer your questions Beatifically smiling as he sends another packed dancefloor into raptures, Carl Cox is one of the most enduring and reliably euphoria-inducing figures in UK club culture history. As he prepares to close out the current season at Drumsheds, the UK’s biggest nightclub, and looks towards a return of his residency at Ibiza nightclub Unvrs, he will join us to answer your questions. Known for playing a banging yet nuanced blend of house and techno, Cox’s career stretches back to the age of 10, learning his craft growing up in London and later Brighton, funding nights out by trimming his neighbours’ hedges. As Chicago house, Detroit techno and other new styles hit the UK, Cox was primed to receive them: fluidly mixing across three decks at once, he immersed himself in both the illegal rave scene and the new wave of nightclubs cropping up to showcase this music. Continue reading...

articles.content: Regulator Ofgem announces that the typical annual gas and electricity bill will rise by 26% in January – described as ‘deeply worrying’ by campaigners Hannah Webster , senior economist at the think tank New Economics Foundation , also called for other measures. The price cap increase will be difficult news for households to bear, especially during the winter when our energy needs and bills are higher. The government’s current support measures don’t match the reality of rising costs and squeezed household finances. The £100 payment announced at the budget won’t cover the increase that’s coming, nor is it available to every household. According to NEF analysis, one million low-income households will miss out. Today’s price cap rise shows how exposed households remain to imported energy - the answer is to generate more at home. Biomethane, made from farms and food waste, is already flowing through our grid - enough to heat around a million homes - but NESO [National Energy System Operator] has just cut its outlook for biomethane because of policy uncertainty. Continue reading...

articles.content: Machines are bulldozing through hard problems to assert the power of their tech bro creators, not to advance human knowledge In most walks of life, trying something 12,363,153,437,138 times and getting the same result is reason enough to assume it works every time. Not in maths, where a conjecture that holds up more than 12tn times looks very probably true but doesn’t qualify as proven. That was the status of the Riemann hypothesis, one of the most famous mathematical conundrums in existence, until last week . Then Levent Alpöge, a mathematician working at Anthropic, said he and his collaborator, Claude AI, had crossed the line from conjecture to proof. Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnist Continue reading...

articles.author: Sali Hughes
articles.content: These fragrances are on trend right now, and smelling creamy can, it turns out, be surprisingly pleasant When the fragrance world picks a theme, it goes in hard. In the space of one month, I had close to a dozen new “lactonic” (that is, milky or creamy themed) perfumes to try. Instinctively, I wasn’t keen – I haven’t touched a glass of milk since nursery school – and so I eased myself in with DedCool’s Mocha Magic (£24 for 15ml), which adds a shot of coffee to the brand’s Xtra Milk fragrance that I love. This is immediately creamy, rich and bittersweet, like tiramisu, right down to that same dry hit of cocoa powder at the back of the throat. As in life, the coffee wears off, but the vanilla, spice and woody notes hang around for an impressively long spell. As with almost everything right now, it’s sweet, but not overbearingly so. Phlur, so beloved by gen Z, has leapt onboard the trend with Heavy Cream (from £26), available in fragrance and scented body spray. This is creamy, obviously, but also very sweet and immediately brings to mind Swizzels Drumstick lollies and the retro fizzy drink American cream soda. If this sounds like a kids’ party from hell, blame me, because it’s actually perfectly pleasant, got me heaps of compliments and got better and mellower as the hours passed. If you’re a milk with three sugars sort of a person, I think you may love it. Continue reading...

articles.author: Adrian Horton
articles.content: Writer-director Beth de Araújo witnessed a brutal sexual assault as a child and has turned her experience into one of the year’s most powerful movies The film-maker Beth de Araújo likens the personal experience that inspired Josephine, her disquieting second feature, to a slow-acting poison. Early one Saturday morning when she was eight years old, Araújo and her father were playing soccer in Golden Gate Park, near their home in San Francisco, when they heard a woman scream. Her father, a former Olympic runner for Brazil, told her to stay and bolted to help; Araújo, scared and alone, ran after him, and instead found the woman in a clearing, naked from the waist down. Araújo was too young to understand what had happened, but she knew something was wrong. So, too, does an eight-year-old Josephine, played by the remarkable newcomer Mason Reeves, in the one scene crafted exactly to Araújo’s memory: Josephine, confused and restless, observes as the woman tucks her hands under her legs to keep them from shaking. She is further confused when her father, Damien, played by the aspirationally everyman actor Channing Tatum, seems extra keen to return to their soccer game afterwards, one of many echoes of Araújo’s memory in this taut drama. In real life, Araújo’s father “put on a face, put on energy and made it seem fun,” she recalled. “And I was like: ‘This is so weird. Why is my dad being so extra fun right now?’” Continue reading...

articles.content: The pair, who met in 2010, are shown preparing for the Dublin race to raise awareness of Fogarty’s epidermolysis bullosa in Rachel Fleit’s considerate documentary The personal scenes in this film from Rachel Fleit have been carefully controlled and curated, the privacy of both parties being important, for different and understandable reasons. But it is an unexpectedly intimate, emotional piece of work, a big-hearted odd-couple story, which is perhaps slightly more complex than at first appears. Emma Fogarty is a smart, garrulous woman from Abbeyleix in County Laois in the Republic of Ireland who has EB: epidermolysis bullosa, a rare condition which means that her skin is permanently, agonisingly painful and requires a daily calvary of bandaging and re-bandaging. While getting an award at the People of the year event in 2010 for her campaigning work educating the public about this illness, Emma met and struck up a friendship with Colin Farrell, a supporter and patron of the EB charity Debra Ireland . Continue reading...

articles.author: Leander Schaerlaeckens
articles.content: The job of Mauricio Pochettino’s successor is to fine-tune a team on the up. That requires a bureaucrat rather than a figurehead First, let’s get the Pep Exception out of the way. Or perhaps we’d better call it the Guardiola Caveat. Regardless, the point is the same. If US Soccer can get Pep Guardiola to manage the United States men’s national team, it should. Because when you have the chance to employ the most successful and influential coach of his generation, the thinker who stands upstream of essentially every major tactical current of the last two decades, you just have to do it. But let us assume that US Soccer can’t appoint Guardiola, because he is only a few months into his post-Manchester City sabbatical and still busying himself defending his body of work . Because he has given no recent indication that he wants the job, even though he spent a previous break between managerial gigs living in New York City and was probably only being supportive of his newly-appointed colleague Mauricio Pochettino when he called the project “fascinating” two years ago. Also because he has only ever signed on to coach teams stacked with Ballon d’Or contenders, posing a Phil Jackson-type, bar-room question over whether he would still be exceptional in charge of unexceptional players. Then again, Guardiola says he expects his next job to be in international management, if and when he does return. Continue reading...

articles.author: Yagnishsing Dawoor
articles.content: The Norwegian Nobel laureate’s sequel to Vaim explores what happens when a man is stripped of everything that tells him who he is Very strange things happen in Jon Fosse’s 2025 novel Vaim . A man meets a woman he secretly loved in his youth while running an errand in a nearby town. She asks him to take her away with him, to the place where they both grew up, on the boat he named after her. She wants to live with him, she tells him, even though she is married, and he has never admitted his feelings. This same man, in another section, has now died. The woman returns to her husband, and tells him he must get back with her, but he has to answer to the name she gave him when they lived together. He must also move into the home of the man she had left him for. “All was strange,” the husband admits, and decides those words should be on his tombstone. Indeed, all is – and remains – very strange to the reader: the powerlessness of these men before this woman they hardly seem to know; the randomness of the events in their lives; their spooky, dream-like surreality. But most of all: Fosse’s narrative choices that thwart easy rationalisation. Vaim Hotel is the second volume in the Nobel laureate’s loosely connected trilogy-in-progress set in the fictional Norwegian town of Vaim. Told in Fosse’s hypnotically recursive style, in a nimble translation by Damion Searls, it is ostensibly a tale of captivity that is only a touch less disorienting than its predecessor, thanks in part to the thematic correspondences it establishes. Beckettian in its relish for the absurd and the tediously mundane, this single-sentence novel opens with a man in his 50s who, for reasons he cannot quite explain, drives to Vaim, and decides to lodge at the empty Vaim Hotel, as yet unaware that he might never leave. Here, too, we have a mysterious female figure before whom male agency fails: Brita, owner of the hotel. Continue reading...

articles.author: Jack Seale
articles.content: In this adaptation of the sci-fi franchise Michelle Yeoh and Hunter Schafer are on a quest to track down a group of replicants gone rogue. It’s a neon-filled world of beautiful doomsday visions Memory: the mother of the muses, and the heart of the Blade Runner franchise. Science fiction is forever asking what it means to be human and, in the future dystopia first painted by Ridley Scott’s 1982 movie, the answer is that we are what we remember: we are the experiences we preserve as a collection of short films inside our heads. In the original Blade Runner, Rachael (Sean Young) is devastated to learn that her childhood memories aren’t real, and she is therefore a robot “replicant”; in Denis Villeneuve’s sequel, Blade Runner 2049, K (Ryan Gosling) knows he’s a replicant but hopes his memories are a sign that he is something close to human. Blade Runner has always been relevant to the age of AI, in that its starting point is that enslaved robots have rebelled. But the new version, the story’s first expansion into television, is acutely topical in an era where we’re increasingly anxious about whether what we’re seeing – or reading – is the work of machines. Fifty years on from the events of the last movie, the replicants have won: “Blade runners” are now replicants hunting down disobedient humans rather than the other way around, and the capture and storage of human memories is illegal. As humanity dies, what it remembers has become valuable contraband. Continue reading...

articles.content: A new book charts the complicated relationship between the two legends, starting on a sunny afternoon in Rio in 1979 Pelé and Diego Maradona first met in April 1979, not long after the Argentinian led his country’s under-20 side to the finals of the World Youth Cup. Maradona told a journalist friend that his dream was to meet the Brazilian, and after a few weeks of aborted attempts to bring them together – mostly because Diego did not want to travel on a Monday, the one day he had free for his girlfriend Claudia – the meeting finally took place in Rio. Reporter Guillermo Blanco, who was writing about the meeting for Argentinian sports magazine El Gráfico, got the OK from Pelé’s people and was so intent on making it happen that he checked Maradona onto a flight one Sunday night without telling him. He collared the young man after Argentine Juniors played Huracán and then raced to the airport and put him on a plane with his father, his agent and a photographer. Continue reading...

articles.content: Four umpires discuss how they deal with players, why they avoid social media, how technology is changing cricket and why umpiring beats being a football referee By Wisden Cricket Monthly Last summer, sat in a quiet ground at the fag-end of a four-dayer, with a few souls still kicking around and a clutch of cameras streaming what was left of the day live on YouTube, it struck me again what a great, strange sanctuary this place is, out there on the edges of the modern world. The game is trying to move, albeit at its own pace. Later that night, the day’s highlights would be landing on social media, available to all, for the game’s devotees to pore over and pick apart. More people are watching the County Championship than ever before. Streaming numbers show a growing audience in the UK and a widening uptake across the cricketing globe. The numbers aren’t yet earth-shattering, but how could they be, with such eccentric fare? Continue reading...

articles.content: Plus: the quickest team to go from FA Cup winners to the first round and matches delayed by snowball fights Mail us with all of your questions and answers “Ronaldinho played for Ravenna, in Serie C, earlier this month. It was his first professional appearance in more than 11 years,” writes George Jones. “Have any other footballers had long career hiatuses? And has any player had a longer hiatus than 11 years?” Ronaldinho’s last professional appearance before his return for Ravenna came on 26 September 2015 for Fluminense, who won 2-0 at home against Goiás. He was withdrawn after 45 minutes. Fans of symmetry will be pleased to see that 11 years and 50 days later, the Brazilian returned for Ravenna in a 2-0 home win against another team with five letters and an accent in their name, Forlì, and was withdrawn after 45 minutes.
